Data science is mostly not modelling. It is getting the data, trusting it, describing it honestly, and saying what it cannot answer. This file is DOM207's thirteen modules as a roadmap, the reference to work from, and thirty-nine problems — the same thirty-nine that appear in the R file.

    Start here

    In plain terms

    Four modes, thirteen modules and thirty-nine problems is a lot to open cold. This is the order to meet them in. It is a suggestion, not a schedule: nothing in this file has a deadline in it.

    Ten days, in order, through material that is already in this file. Every step is a link — nothing here is a separate checklist, so your coverage percentage means the same thing before and after you use it.

    1. First hourGet the tools running and no more: the setup section, then one script that prints a number. Do not install anything you have not been asked for yet.
    2. First hourRead Reading an error message before you need it. The rows marked silent matter most — those are the ones that hand you a wrong number without complaining.
    3. Day 1Set M01, three problems. Then open the same three in the other language's file and solve them again. That doubling is the whole method of this course, and it is easiest to start on the day the problems are simple.
    4. Day 2Getting data in: read a CSV, look at what arrived, describe it. Set M03. Run .info() or str() on every file you ever open, before anything else.
    5. Day 3Cleaning, set M04. Slower than it looks and the biggest single share of real project time. Write down every decision as you make it — the writeup needs them and you will not remember.
    6. Day 4Visualisation, set M05. Label every axis with a unit from the first chart you draw; going back to add them later never happens.
    7. Days 5&ndash;6Control flow and functions, sets M06 and M07. Then stop and write one function you actually reuse. That is the point of the pair of sets.
    8. Day 7Distributions and correlation, set M08, and read Which test do I use once through even though you have not met half of it yet. It is the map for the next two weeks.
    9. Days 8&ndash;9Hypothesis tests, set M09. This is the material the End Sem leans on hardest, and Gen AI is banned in that paper — so answer the recall questions in this set out loud before you tick them.
    10. Day 10Regression, set M10. The most useful technique on the syllabus. After this the roadmap takes over from this list — and read the same thing in both languages whenever you are stuck translating between the two files.

    If you are following the course rather than starting from scratch, ignore this and jump to the module you are on — the sets are numbered to match.

    ◆

    The roadmap

    Ten stages tracking DOM207 · Introduction to Data Science (Monsoon 2026) module by module, extended with the career-relevant topics from roadmap.sh's Python for Data Analysis path. The course teaches Python and R in lockstep on the same topics, so this file and r.html mirror each other — the R file is not a lesser version. Modules are numbered, not dated, because a real course drifts from its outline and a roadmap that insists otherwise is arguing with reality. Hour figures are estimates from topic count, not measurements.

    Stage 01

    Setup and the language

    DOM207 modules 1, 3, 6 and 7. The course assumes no programming experience, so this stage is the whole language — and it is the stage where falling behind is most expensive, because everything later assumes it.

    In plain terms

    Getting the tools installed and writing your first few lines. No data science yet — just enough of the language that the rest of the file reads as English.

    modules 1 · 3 · 6 · 7~30–40 h

    1.1 · A working environment

    Deliverable: the interpreter running a script from a file, not just a REPL

    • Python installed; python3 --version runs
    • A virtual environment: python3 -m venv .venv
    • pip install pandas numpy matplotlib seaborn scipy scikit-learn statsmodels
    • Jupyter or Spyder, and running a .py file directly
    • Reading a traceback from the bottom up

    1.2 · Types and vectors

    Deliverable: a script that builds, indexes and summarises a numeric collection

    • int, float, str, bool, None
    • Lists, tuples, dicts, sets
    • Indexing and slicing; 0-based
    • NumPy arrays and vectorised arithmetic
    • None vs np.nan
    • Dates with datetime / pd.to_datetime
    • f-strings and str methods

    1.3 · Control flow and functions

    Deliverable: a reusable function with default arguments, called from another script

    • if / elif / else
    • for and while
    • Vectorised operations instead of loops
    • def, positional and keyword arguments, defaults
    • Return values, and returning a tuple
    • List comprehensions
    • Docstrings and why the function needs one
    Stage 02

    Getting data in

    DOM207 module 4. The tabular structure and the four or five ways data arrives. In consulting the file is almost always someone's Excel export, so the awkward cases matter more than the clean ones.

    In plain terms

    Data starts life in a file somebody else made. This stage is opening it, seeing what actually arrived, and describing it in numbers before changing anything.

    module 4~15–20 h

    2.1 · The tabular type

    Deliverable: a data frame built by hand, indexed three different ways

    • pd.DataFrame and pd.Series
    • .loc vs .iloc — label vs position
    • Boolean filtering
    • Adding and dropping columns
    • Matrices and arrays where they still apply

    2.2 · Reading real files

    Deliverable: the same dataset loaded from CSV and from Excel, verified identical

    • pd.read_csv — separators, encodings, na_values
    • pd.read_excel and sheet selection
    • Headers that are not on row 1
    • JSON and Parquet, for when it is not a spreadsheet
    • Writing results back out

    2.3 · Describing what arrived

    Deliverable: a one-screen summary of a real dataset: shape, types, missingness, ranges

    • .shape, .dtypes, .info()
    • .describe()
    • Mean, median, mode, range, IQR
    • .value_counts() for categoricals
    • .groupby().agg()
    Stage 03

    Cleaning and exploring

    DOM207 module 2, and the part of the job that actually consumes the time. Every decision here changes the answer, so every one of them belongs in the writeup.

    In plain terms

    Real data has missing entries, duplicate rows and three spellings of the same word. Cleaning is deciding what to do about each — on the record, because every one of those choices moves a number in your final answer.

    module 2~25–30 hmost of the real work

    3.1 · Missing data

    Deliverable: a documented decision per column: dropped, imputed, or left missing — with the reason

    • .isna(), .isna().sum()
    • .dropna() — and what it silently removes
    • .fillna(): mean, median, forward fill
    • Whether missingness is itself informative
    • na.rm / skipna and the default that bites

    3.2 · Types, strings and duplicates

    Deliverable: a dataset where every column has the type it should have

    • .astype() and pd.to_numeric(errors=)
    • .str.strip(), .replace(), .split()
    • Regular expressions, at least the basics
    • .duplicated() / .drop_duplicates()
    • Categoricals and pd.get_dummies

    3.3 · Outliers and shape

    Deliverable: an EDA notebook that ends in three specific questions worth testing

    • IQR rule and z-scores
    • Visual inspection before any rule
    • Deciding to keep, cap or drop — and saying which
    • .merge() and join types
    • .pivot() / .melt() — wide and long
    Stage 04

    Visualisation

    DOM207 module 5. In consulting this is the deliverable, not a step toward it — the chart is what the client remembers.

    In plain terms

    Drawing the data. Half to find things you would never have spotted in a table of numbers, half because a chart is what you actually hand over at the end.

    module 5~20–25 h

    4.1 · The four charts that carry most work

    Deliverable: histogram, boxplot, scatter and bar, each saved to a file

    • Histogram, and choosing bins honestly
    • Boxplot, and what the whiskers actually mean
    • Scatter, and overplotting
    • Bar chart vs histogram — a real distinction
    • Saving at a resolution that survives a slide deck

    4.2 · The grammar

    Deliverable: one figure with facets, a legend and axis labels a client could read unaided

    • matplotlib figure and axes objects
    • seaborn for statistical plots
    • Subplots and small multiples
    • Colour, and not encoding meaning in it alone
    • Titles, units and source notes on every chart
    Stage 05

    Statistics and inference

    DOM207 modules 8 and 9. The step from describing the sample to making a claim about the population — and the point where being wrong stops being visible in the output.

    In plain terms

    Asking whether a pattern in your sample is strong enough to say something about the world, or whether chance alone would produce it often enough that reporting it would be misleading.

    modules 8 · 9~30–35 h

    5.1 · Distributions and relationships

    Deliverable: a fitted normal overlaid on a real histogram, with the mismatch discussed

    • Normal, binomial, Poisson — and when each applies
    • PDF, CDF, quantiles
    • Correlation: Pearson vs Spearman
    • Covariance matrices
    • Correlation is not causation — and what would establish it

    5.2 · Hypothesis tests

    Deliverable: a two-sample comparison with the test choice justified in writing

    • Null and alternative, stated before looking
    • One-sample and two-sample t-tests
    • Welch's test, and why it is the better default
    • Ansari–Bradley for differences in spread
    • One-way ANOVA and post-hoc tests
    • Confidence intervals, and plotting means with them
    • What a p-value is not
    Stage 06

    Regression — the analyst ceiling

    DOM207 module 10. Multiple regression done properly, with the diagnostics, is the single most useful technique on this list. A consulting deliverable is far more often this than anything below it.

    In plain terms

    Fitting a line through the data so you can say how much one thing moves when another does, and how confident that estimate is. This is as far as most analyst jobs go, and it is the most useful thing on this syllabus.

    module 10~30–40 hthe payoff stage
    Where the analyst stops and the modeller startsEverything above this line is what a consulting case actually asks for: get the data, trust it, describe it, test a claim, and quantify a relationship. Everything below is modelling — worth learning, and DOM207 examines it, but a client deliverable is far more often a clean regression with its assumptions checked than a neural network. DOM207 puts this boundary between module 10 and module 11.

    6.1 · OLS and what it assumes

    Deliverable: a multiple regression reported with coefficients, CIs, R² and adjusted R²

    • statsmodels OLS with a formula
    • Reading the coefficient table
    • R² vs adjusted R², and why the second exists
    • Confidence intervals on coefficients
    • Dummy variables and the reference category
    • Interaction terms

    6.2 · Diagnostics — the part people skip

    Deliverable: a residual plot, a VIF table, and a written statement of which assumption is strained

    • Residual plots, and what a pattern means
    • Normality of residuals — Q-Q plot
    • Heteroskedasticity, and robust standard errors
    • Multicollinearity and VIF
    • Influential points: leverage and Cook's distance
    • Model specification: omitted variables, wrong functional form

    6.3 · When the outcome is not continuous

    Deliverable: a logistic regression with odds ratios interpreted in plain sentences

    • Maximum likelihood, conceptually
    • Logit — and reading an odds ratio
    • Probit, and how it differs in practice
    • Poisson regression for counts
    • Predicted probabilities rather than raw coefficients
    Stage 07

    Text analytics and trees

    DOM207 module 11. The first stage past the analyst line. Text is where most business data actually lives — tickets, reviews, open-ended survey answers.

    In plain terms

    Two things the earlier tools cannot do: turning written words into numbers you can analyse, and fitting a model that works by asking a series of yes/no questions.

    module 11~20–25 h

    7.1 · Turning text into numbers

    Deliverable: a TF-IDF matrix over a real set of documents, with the top terms per document listed

    • Tokenisation, case folding, stop words
    • Stemming vs lemmatisation
    • Term frequency, document frequency, TF-IDF
    • The document-term matrix
    • Why TF-IDF beats raw counts

    7.2 · Decision trees

    Deliverable: a fitted tree, plotted, with the top split explained in one sentence

    • How a split is chosen: Gini and entropy
    • Depth, pruning and overfitting
    • Reading a tree as a set of rules
    • Feature importance, and its instability
    • Trees as the interpretable model clients accept
    Stage 08

    Unsupervised learning

    DOM207 module 12. Structure without a label — segmentation, which is the single most requested piece of analysis in commercial consulting.

    In plain terms

    Finding structure in data that has no answer column — grouping similar rows together, or squeezing many columns down to a few that carry most of the information.

    module 12~20–25 h

    8.1 · Clustering

    Deliverable: a k-means segmentation with k justified by an elbow or silhouette, not chosen by eye

    • k-means, and why scaling first is mandatory
    • Choosing k: elbow, silhouette, Hartigan's rule
    • Hierarchical clustering and linkage
    • Reading a dendrogram and cutting it
    • Naming clusters from their centroids — the deliverable

    8.2 · Dimensionality reduction

    Deliverable: a PCA with a scree plot and the first two components interpreted

    • PCA, and standardising before it
    • Explained variance and the scree plot
    • Loadings, and naming a component
    • PCA as pre-processing for clustering
    • What PCA destroys: interpretability of the originals
    Stage 09

    Supervised learning and networks

    DOM207 module 13, which is a whirlwind: SVM, neural networks, backpropagation, deep learning and LLMs in one week. Treat the exam-relevant part as conceptual and the code part as train/test discipline.

    In plain terms

    Learning a rule from examples where you already know the answer, applying it to cases where you do not, and — the part that carries the marks — telling whether it will actually hold up on data it has never seen.

    module 13~30–40 hbroadest module

    9.1 · Doing supervised learning honestly

    Deliverable: a classifier reported with a confusion matrix on held-out data, never on training data

    • Train/test split, and why it comes first
    • Cross-validation
    • Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 — and when accuracy lies
    • The confusion matrix
    • Overfitting, and the bias–variance trade-off
    • Leakage — the mistake that produces suspiciously good results

    9.2 · SVM and neural networks

    Deliverable: an SVM and a small neural net on the same data, compared on the same held-out split

    • SVM: the margin, and the kernel trick
    • Scaling for SVM — mandatory, same as k-means
    • A neuron, a layer, an activation function
    • Backpropagation, conceptually
    • Why depth helps, and what it costs in interpretability
    • LLMs: transformer, attention, pre-train then fine-tune
    • When a simpler model is the correct professional answer
    Stage 10

    The project

    DOM207's project is 45% of the grade — more than the End Sem — and Gen AI assistance is explicitly permitted on it. This stage is the structure the course's own learning outcomes ask for.

    In plain terms

    Forty-five percent of your grade. Not a new technique: a question worth asking, a method you can defend, and a report somebody else can check.

    45% of the gradeAI-assist allowed~25–40 h

    10.1 · Framing, before any code

    Deliverable: a one-page brief: purpose statement, central question, sub-questions, and the method for each

    • Define a problem suitable for analytics
    • Identify variables and their level of measurement
    • Write a purpose statement
    • One central question, three or four sub-questions
    • Match each sub-question to a specific method
    • State what would falsify your expected answer

    10.2 · Doing it reproducibly

    Deliverable: a script that runs start to finish on a clean machine and regenerates every number in the report

    • One script, top to bottom, no manual steps
    • Raw data untouched; all changes in code
    • Set a random seed and say so
    • Every cleaning decision recorded with its reason
    • Figures regenerated by the script, not pasted

    10.3 · Reporting it

    Deliverable: a deck or memo where every number traces to a line of code and every limit is stated

    • Lead with the finding, not the method
    • Effect size and interval, not just significance
    • State the limits beside the claim, not in a footnote
    • Say what the data cannot answer
    • One chart per point, labelled to stand alone
    • A recommendation the client can actually act on

    0x01

    Setup & running code

    In plain terms

    Before you can run anything you need Python itself, plus the extra libraries this course uses. A virtual environment is just a folder holding one project's own copies of those libraries, so installing something for this course cannot break something else on your machine.

    DOM207 lets you use IDLE, Spyder, Jupyter or Anaconda. Whichever you pick, the thing that matters is that your work runs top to bottom in a fresh session — a notebook that only works if you run the cells out of order is not a result you can defend.

    Environment and packages

    # a project-local environment
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate.fish   # fish
source .venv/bin/activate        # bash/zsh

pip install pandas numpy matplotlib seaborn \
            scipy scikit-learn statsmodels
pip freeze > requirements.txt

    A virtual environment keeps one project's package versions from breaking another's. requirements.txt is what makes the analysis reproducible on a different machine — including the marker's.

    Record versions. A pandas 2 script can behave differently on pandas 3, and "it worked on my laptop" is not a defence in a report.

    Running it

    python3 analysis.py          # a script, start to finish
python3 -i analysis.py       # then drop into a REPL
jupyter lab                  # notebook

# in a notebook, before you trust anything:
# Kernel -> Restart & Run All

    Notebooks keep hidden state: a variable defined in a cell you later deleted is still in memory. Restart-and-run-all is the only way to know the notebook actually produces its own output.

    For the project, keep a plain .py that regenerates every number and figure. The notebook is for exploring; the script is the deliverable.

    Reading a traceback

    Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "analysis.py", line 42, in <module>
    total = df["revenu"].sum()
            ~~^^^^^^^^^^
KeyError: 'revenu'

    Read it bottom up. The last line names the error type and value; the lines above are the call chain that reached it, most recent last. The caret marks the exact expression.

    A KeyError on a column name is nearly always a typo or trailing whitespace in the header. df.columns.tolist() settles it in one line.

    Imports, by convention

    import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

    These aliases are near-universal. Following them means any example you find online drops into your code unchanged, and anyone reading yours knows immediately what pd is.

    Never from pandas import *. It dumps hundreds of names into your namespace and something will shadow a builtin you were relying on.

    0x02

    Types & operators

    In plain terms

    A type is what kind of value something is: a whole number, a number with a decimal point, a piece of text, a yes/no. Python works the type out for you as it goes, but it will not guess across kinds — adding text to a number is an error, not a coincidence it will paper over.

    Python's types are dynamic but not weak — it will refuse to add a string to a number rather than guessing. Most surprises here come from division, floating point, and the two different meanings of equality.

    The basic types

    n    = 42              # int, unbounded
x    = 3.14            # float, 64-bit
s    = "text"          # str, immutable
flag = True            # bool (a subclass of int!)
none = None            # absence of a value

type(n), isinstance(n, int)
int("42"), float("3.5"), str(42)
True + True            # 2 — bool really is an int

    Integers have no size limit, so factorials and large counts never silently overflow the way they do in C. Floats are IEEE-754 doubles with all the usual consequences.

    bool subclassing int is why sum([True, False, True]) returns 2 — which is genuinely useful for counting how many rows match a condition.

    Operators worth knowing

    7 / 2     # 3.5  — always float
7 // 2    # 3    — floor division
7 % 2     # 1
2 ** 10   # 1024

a == b    # equal value
a is b    # the same object

x if cond else y        # ternary
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3        # False!
abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < 1e-9   # the right test

    / always produces a float, which is the opposite of C and of Python 2. Comparing floats with == fails for the usual binary-representation reasons.

    Use is only for None, True and False. x is 1000 may be False even when x == 1000, because small integers are interned and large ones are not.

    Strings and f-strings

    name, rev = "North", 12345.678

f"{name}: {rev:,.2f}"      # North: 12,345.68
f"{rev:>12.1f}"            # right-aligned, width 12
f"{0.4567:.1%}"            # 45.7%
f"{name=}"                 # name='North' — debugging

s.strip().lower().replace(",", "")
s.split(",")
",".join(["a", "b"])
"North" in s               # substring test

    f-strings do formatting inline, which keeps the value next to its format. :, for thousands separators and :.1% for percentages cover most reporting needs.

    Strings are immutable — every method returns a new string. s.strip() on its own line does nothing; you must assign the result.

    None, NaN and missing

    None is None          # True
np.nan == np.nan      # False — NaN equals nothing
np.isnan(np.nan)      # True
pd.isna(None)         # True
pd.isna(np.nan)       # True

    Three different absences: None is Python's null, np.nan is a float value meaning "not a number", and pandas treats both as missing. pd.isna is the one that handles all cases.

    NaN != NaN is by IEEE design, which is why filtering with df[df.col == np.nan] silently returns zero rows. Always df[df.col.isna()].

    0x03

    Collections

    In plain terms

    A collection holds several values in one variable. The four here differ in whether order matters, whether you fetch things by position or by name, and whether repeats are allowed. Choose by how you will get the values back out again.

    Four built-in containers with genuinely different jobs. Choosing the wrong one is rarely a bug and often the difference between code that reads clearly and code that does not.

    list, tuple, dict, set

    xs = [1, 2, 3]              # mutable, ordered
pt = (10.5, 20.1)           # immutable, ordered
d  = {"north": 120, "south": 95}   # key -> value
s  = {1, 2, 3}              # unique, unordered

xs.append(4); xs.extend([5, 6])
d["east"] = 80; d.get("west", 0)   # default, no KeyError
d.keys(), d.values(), d.items()
set(a) & set(b)             # intersection

    Use a tuple when the thing has a fixed shape — a coordinate, a return of two values. Use a dict as soon as you find yourself remembering what position 3 means. A set answers "have I seen this" in constant time.

    d.get(k, default) instead of d[k] whenever the key might be absent. It is the difference between a default and a crash.

    Slicing

    xs = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

xs[0]      # 10   first (0-based)
xs[-1]     # 50   last
xs[1:3]    # [20, 30]  stop is EXCLUSIVE
xs[:2]     # [10, 20]
xs[::2]    # [10, 30, 50]  step
xs[::-1]   # reversed

    The stop index is always exclusive, which is why xs[a:b] has exactly b - a elements and xs[:k] + xs[k:] reconstructs the original.

    Coming from R this is the biggest adjustment: 0-based, and the upper bound not included. R's x[1:3] is three elements; Python's is two.

    Comprehensions

    sq   = [x**2 for x in range(10)]
even = [x for x in xs if x % 2 == 0]
caps = {k: v.upper() for k, v in d.items()}
uniq = {w.lower() for w in words}

# nested, read left to right as nested loops
pairs = [(a, b) for a in "AB" for b in [1, 2]]

    A comprehension is the idiomatic replacement for a loop that builds a list. It is shorter, faster, and makes the intent — "a new list from this one" — visible at a glance.

    Stop at one level of nesting and one condition. Past that, a real loop is clearer, and clarity beats compactness in code someone will grade.

    Copying, and the trap

    a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a            # SAME list, not a copy
b.append(4)
a                # [1, 2, 3, 4] — a changed too

c = a.copy()     # shallow copy
import copy
d = copy.deepcopy(nested)   # nested structures

    Assignment binds a second name to the same object; it never copies. For immutable types this is invisible, and for lists and dicts it produces action at a distance.

    A mutable default argument — def f(x, acc=[]) — is evaluated once at definition and shared across every call. Use acc=None and build inside.

    0x04

    Control flow & functions

    In plain terms

    Two ideas. Control flow is how you say “only do this if…” and “do this once for each of these”. A function is a named block of code you can run again later with different values, so you write it once.

    DOM207 modules 6 and 7. The syntax is small; the judgement is knowing when a loop is the wrong tool, which in data work is most of the time.

    Conditions and loops

    if score >= 80:
    band = "High"
elif score >= 60:
    band = "Medium"
else:
    band = "Low"

for i, name in enumerate(names):
    print(i, name)

for a, b in zip(xs, ys):
    ...

while balance <= target and year < 200:
    ...

    Indentation is the block structure — there are no braces and no end. enumerate and zip remove almost every reason to loop over an index.

    Python has no switch. A dict of handlers, or match in 3.10+, replaces a long elif chain.

    Functions

    def cv(x, ddof=1):
    """Coefficient of variation: sd / mean.

    Unitless, so it compares spread across
    variables measured in different units.
    """
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    m = x.mean()
    return np.nan if m == 0 else x.std(ddof=ddof) / m

cv(values)                # positional
cv(values, ddof=0)        # keyword — clearer

def stats(x):
    return {"mean": ..., "sd": ...}   # named results

    The docstring should say what the output means, not restate the code. "Unitless, so it compares across variables" is useful; "computes the coefficient of variation" is not.

    Return a dict rather than a bare tuple once there are more than two results. s["sd"] survives a reordering that s[2] does not.

    Vectorise instead

    # slow: interpreted loop per row
out = []
for v in df["revenue"]:
    out.append(v * 1.18)

# fast: one compiled operation
df["with_gst"] = df["revenue"] * 1.18

# conditional, vectorised
df["band"] = np.where(df.score >= 80, "High", "Low")
df["band"] = np.select(
    [df.score >= 80, df.score >= 60],
    ["High", "Medium"], default="Low")

    A loop over rows runs the Python interpreter once per row; the vectorised form runs compiled C once over the whole array. On 100,000 rows that is typically a 50–100× difference.

    If you are writing for over df.iterrows(), there is almost always a vectorised form. iterrows is also slow and loses dtypes.

    Errors, deliberately

    try:
    df = pd.read_csv(path)
except FileNotFoundError:
    print(f"missing: {path}")
    raise                 # re-raise, do not swallow

assert len(df) > 0, "empty dataset"

    Catch the specific exception, not bare except:. A bare except catches typos, keyboard interrupts and genuine bugs alike, and turns them into silence.

    In an analysis script, failing loudly is better than continuing with bad data. A crash you see beats a number you trust and should not.

    0x05

    NumPy

    In plain terms

    NumPy adds one thing: an array, meaning many numbers held together and operated on as a unit. x * 2 doubles every element with no loop anywhere. Everything else in the data stack is built on top of it, which is why it is worth meeting before pandas.

    The array type everything else is built on. pandas columns are NumPy arrays, scikit-learn takes and returns them, and every vectorised operation in Python data work is ultimately a NumPy operation.

    Creating arrays

    np.array([1, 2, 3])
np.zeros(5); np.ones((2, 3)); np.full(3, 7)
np.arange(0, 10, 2)        # [0 2 4 6 8]
np.linspace(0, 1, 5)       # 5 points inclusive

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)   # seeded
rng.normal(50, 10, 100)
rng.uniform(0, 1, 100)
rng.integers(1, 7, 10)
rng.choice(["A", "B"], 20)

    default_rng(seed) is the modern generator API and the one to use; the older np.random.seed plus np.random.normal shares global state across your whole program.

    Seed every simulation and say so in the report. An unseeded result cannot be reproduced by the person marking it.

    Vectorised maths

    a * 2; a + b; a ** 2; np.sqrt(a); np.log(a)

a.sum(); a.mean(); a.std(ddof=1); a.min()
a.argmax()                 # position of the max
np.median(a); np.percentile(a, [25, 75])

m.sum(axis=0)              # down columns
m.sum(axis=1)              # across rows

    axis=0 collapses rows and gives you one value per column; axis=1 collapses columns. Remembering it as "the axis that disappears" is the reliable mnemonic.

    std() defaults to ddof=0 — the population version. R's sd() and pandas' .std() both use ddof=1. Pass it explicitly whenever a number will be compared across tools.

    Boolean masks

    mask = a > 50
a[mask]                    # the values that pass
mask.sum()                 # how many passed
mask.mean()                # the proportion

a[(a > 20) & (a < 80)]     # & and |, NOT and/or
np.where(a > 50, "high", "low")

    A boolean array indexes another array of the same shape. Because True is 1, summing a mask counts and averaging it gives a proportion — used constantly for missingness and rates.

    Use & and |, never and/or, and parenthesise each comparison. and raises on arrays, and missing parentheses bind wrongly against the comparison operators.

    Shape and broadcasting

    a.shape; a.ndim; a.dtype; len(a)
a.reshape(3, 4); a.T; a.ravel()

# broadcasting: a length-1 dimension stretches
np.arange(3) + 10          # scalar to all
m + np.array([1, 2, 3])    # row-wise

# shapes that do not broadcast raise, they do not guess

    NumPy stretches dimensions of length 1 and otherwise requires an exact match. That refusal is a feature — R's silent recycling of any divisor-length vector hides genuine mistakes.

    When something "should work" and does not, print .shape first. Nine shape errors in ten are a (n,) where a (n,1) was expected.

    0x06

    pandas — the DataFrame

    In plain terms

    A DataFrame is a table — rows, and columns with names — that you write code against instead of clicking. If you have used a spreadsheet, you already have the mental picture. This is where most of the actual work in this course happens.

    DOM207 module 4. Almost everything you do in applied data science happens here. The DataFrame is a dict of aligned columns, and nearly every confusion comes from forgetting that the index aligns too.

    Reading data in

    df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv",
        sep=";", encoding="latin-1",
        na_values=["", "NA", "-", "n/a"],
        parse_dates=["order_date"],
        dtype={"pin": str})       # keep leading zeros

pd.read_excel("book.xlsx", sheet_name="Q3", skiprows=2)
df.to_csv("out.csv", index=False)

    na_values matters more than it looks: a column where missing was typed as - comes in as text, and every numeric operation on it then fails or silently produces nothing.

    index=False when writing. Without it every round trip adds an unnamed index column, and three round trips give you three of them.

    Looking at it first

    df.shape          # (rows, cols)
df.head(); df.tail(); df.sample(5)
df.info()         # types + non-null counts
df.describe()     # numeric summary
df.describe(include="object")
df.columns.tolist()
df.dtypes
df["region"].value_counts(dropna=False)
df.isna().sum()

    These six lines are the first thing to run on any dataset. info() alone catches the two most common problems: a numeric column read as text, and far more missing values than expected.

    value_counts(dropna=False) — the default hides NaN, which is exactly the category you most need to see early.

    Selecting: loc vs iloc

    df["revenue"]             # one column -> Series
df[["revenue", "units"]]  # several -> DataFrame

df.loc[3, "revenue"]      # by LABEL
df.loc[df.region == "North", ["revenue"]]
df.iloc[0:5, 0:2]         # by POSITION

df[(df.revenue > 100) & (df.region == "North")]
df.query("revenue > 100 and region == 'North'")

    .loc is label-based and its slice end is inclusive; .iloc is position-based and exclusive like normal Python. After a filter, the labels are no longer 0..n, which is where the two diverge painfully.

    Use .reset_index(drop=True) after filtering if you intend to keep using positions. Otherwise .loc[0] may raise on a frame that clearly has rows.

    Group and aggregate

    df.groupby("region")["revenue"].sum()

df.groupby("region").agg(
    total=("revenue", "sum"),
    avg_units=("units", "mean"),
    n=("region", "size"),
).reset_index()

df.groupby(["region", "product"])["revenue"].sum().unstack()
df.pivot_table(index="product", columns="region",
               values="revenue", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0)

    Named aggregation gives output columns that say what they contain. The older dict form leaves a summed column still called revenue, which stops being true the moment someone reads it.

    size counts rows including missing; count counts non-missing. Using the wrong one is a quiet way to report the wrong denominator.

    Joining

    out = sales.merge(lookup, on="code", how="left")
sales.merge(lk, left_on="c", right_on="code", how="inner")

# always check what failed to match
out["region"].isna().sum()
sales.merge(lookup, on="code", how="left",
            indicator=True)["_merge"].value_counts()

    how="left" keeps every row on the left and fills the right with NaN where there was no match. indicator=True adds a column saying which side each row came from.

    Check the row count before and after every join. An unintended many-to-many match multiplies rows and inflates every total downstream, and .head() looks perfectly normal.

    Reshaping

    # wide -> long
long = df.melt(id_vars=["product"],
               value_vars=["q1", "q2", "q3"],
               var_name="quarter", value_name="revenue")

# long -> wide
wide = long.pivot(index="product", columns="quarter",
                  values="revenue").reset_index()

    Long format — one row per observation — is what plotting and modelling libraries expect. Wide format is what people put in spreadsheets and what a report table looks like.

    If a chart or a model is fighting you, check the shape first. Most "seaborn won't plot this" problems are a wide frame that needs melting.

    0x07

    Cleaning

    In plain terms

    Real data arrives broken: entries missing, the same thing spelled three ways, rows recorded twice. Cleaning is deciding what to do about each one. Every decision changes a number further down, so each has to be written down and defensible.

    DOM207 module 2, and where most of the hours go. Every operation here changes a number downstream, so every one of them belongs in the writeup with its reason.

    Missing values

    df.isna().sum()
df.isna().mean().mul(100).round(1)   # % per column

df.dropna()                     # any NaN in the row
df.dropna(subset=["revenue"])   # only this column
df.dropna(thresh=3)             # keep rows with 3+ values

df["revenue"] = df["revenue"].fillna(df["revenue"].median())
df["price"] = df["price"].ffill()    # carry last forward

    Print the count before dropping. dropna() with no arguments removes any row with a missing value anywhere, which on a wide table can be most of the data.

    Imputing shrinks variance and narrows every downstream confidence interval. That is a real cost, so the number of imputed values goes in the report.

    Types and strings

    df["units"] = pd.to_numeric(df["units"], errors="coerce")
# errors="coerce" -> unparseable becomes NaN, not a crash
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"], format="%d/%m/%Y")

df["city"] = df["city"].str.strip().str.title()
df["code"] = df["code"].str.replace(r"\D", "", regex=True)
df["name"].str.contains("ltd", case=False, na=False)
df["full"].str.split(",", expand=True)

    errors="coerce" converts what it can and marks the rest missing — then isna().sum() tells you exactly how many values were unparseable, which is information you want rather than an exception.

    na=False in str.contains. Without it, missing values produce NaN in the mask and the filter raises rather than treating them as non-matches.

    Duplicates and outliers

    df.duplicated().sum()
df = df.drop_duplicates()
df.drop_duplicates(subset=["id"], keep="last")

q1, q3 = df.x.quantile([.25, .75])
iqr = q3 - q1
out = (df.x < q1 - 1.5*iqr) | (df.x > q3 + 1.5*iqr)
df["is_outlier"] = out          # flag, don't delete

z = (df.x - df.x.mean()) / df.x.std()

    Flag outliers as a column rather than removing them. Deleting is a modelling decision that belongs in a later, explicit step — and one you can then defend or reverse.

    1.5 × IQR is a convention tuned to a normal distribution. On skewed data — income, revenue, waiting times — it flags a large number of ordinary values.

    Categoricals

    df["region"] = df["region"].astype("category")
df["region"].cat.categories

# dummies for modelling; drop one to avoid
# perfect collinearity with the intercept
X = pd.get_dummies(df[["region", "size"]], drop_first=True)

pd.cut(df.age, bins=[0, 25, 40, 60, 200],
       labels=["<25", "25-40", "40-60", "60+"])

    drop_first=True leaves k−1 dummies for k categories. Keeping all k alongside an intercept makes the design matrix singular — the "dummy variable trap".

    The dropped category becomes the reference, and every coefficient is then read relative to it. Say which one it is when reporting.

    0x08

    Plotting

    In plain terms

    Drawing charts. matplotlib is the underlying drawing tool and seaborn is a shortcut layer over it for the statistical charts you usually want. Axis labels and units are part of the answer, not decoration added at the end.

    DOM207 module 5. matplotlib is the engine and seaborn is the statistical front end. In consulting the chart is the deliverable, so labelling is not decoration.

    The figure/axes pattern

    import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")     # headless; before pyplot
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5), dpi=150)
ax.plot(x, y, label="2026")
ax.set_xlabel("Spend (Rs lakh)")
ax.set_ylabel("Revenue (Rs lakh)")
ax.set_title("Revenue against spend")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("out.png")
plt.close(fig)

    Work with explicit fig and ax objects rather than the stateful plt.plot interface. Once there is more than one panel, the stateful API becomes ambiguous about which plot you are modifying.

    plt.close(fig) in any loop that makes figures, or matplotlib keeps every one in memory and warns after twenty.

    The charts that carry the work

    ax.hist(x, bins=20, edgecolor="white")
ax.boxplot([a, b, c], tick_labels=["A","B","C"])
ax.scatter(x, y, alpha=0.6, s=18)
ax.bar(names, values)
ax.axhline(0, linewidth=1)
ax.set_ylim(0, None)

    A histogram shows the distribution of one continuous variable; a bar chart shows a value per category. They look similar and answer different questions — mixing them up is a common report error.

    State the bin count on any histogram. It is a choice that changes the shape of the picture, and an unstated choice is an argument the reader cannot check.

    seaborn

    import seaborn as sns

sns.histplot(data=df, x="revenue", hue="region", ax=ax)
sns.boxplot(data=df, x="region", y="revenue", ax=ax)
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="spend", y="revenue",
                hue="region", size="units", ax=ax)
sns.regplot(data=df, x="spend", y="revenue", ax=ax)
sns.heatmap(df.corr(numeric_only=True), annot=True,
            fmt=".2f", ax=ax)

g = sns.catplot(data=df, x="grp", y="v", col="year", kind="box")
g.figure.savefig("facets.png", bbox_inches="tight")

    seaborn takes a long-format DataFrame and column names, and handles grouping and colour itself. Anything ending in plot takes ax=; the figure-level functions (catplot, relplot, lmplot) do not — they create their own figure.

    Figure-level functions return a FacetGrid. Save with g.figure.savefig(...) — calling plt.savefig after one writes a blank figure.

    Charts a client can read

    • Axis labels with units. "Revenue (₹ lakh)", never "revenue".
    • A title that states the finding, not the variables: "Revenue rises 3.2× with spend" beats "Revenue vs spend".
    • Start bar charts at zero. A truncated axis exaggerates every difference.
    • Never encode meaning in colour alone — around 8% of men have some colour-vision deficiency.
    • Source and date in a footnote, so the chart survives being pasted into a deck.

    If a chart needs the surrounding paragraph to be understood, it will be misread the moment someone screenshots it. Make every figure stand alone.

    0x09

    Statistics with SciPy

    In plain terms

    Statistics asks whether a pattern you can see in your sample is strong enough to claim something about the world, or whether ordinary chance would produce it often enough that it is not worth reporting. The code is one line per test; the marks are in choosing the right test and stating what you expected before you looked.

    DOM207 modules 8 and 9. The arithmetic is one line each; the marks are in choosing the right test and stating the hypothesis before you look.

    Distributions

    from scipy import stats

n = stats.norm(loc=100, scale=15)
n.pdf(115)      # density
n.cdf(115)      # P(X <= 115)
n.sf(130)       # P(X > 130), precise in the tail
n.ppf(0.95)     # the 95th percentile
n.rvs(size=100, random_state=1)

stats.binom(n=20, p=0.3).pmf(6)
stats.poisson(mu=4).sf(6)
stats.t(df=29).ppf(0.975)

    Every distribution exposes the same five methods, so learning the pattern once covers all of them. Use sf rather than 1 - cdf in the far tail, where subtraction loses precision.

    For a discrete distribution, sf(6) is P(X > 6) strictly. The difference from P(X ≥ 6) is a whole point of probability mass.

    Correlation

    stats.pearsonr(x, y)      # linear, on values
stats.spearmanr(x, y)     # monotone, on ranks
stats.kendalltau(x, y)

df.corr(numeric_only=True)              # Pearson matrix
df.corr(method="spearman", numeric_only=True)
df.cov(numeric_only=True)

    Pearson only sees straight-line association. A strong curved relationship can show a low Pearson correlation and a high Spearman one — so a low Pearson is not evidence of independence.

    Always plot the scatter as well. Anscombe's quartet is four datasets with identical correlations and completely different shapes.

    Hypothesis tests

    stats.ttest_1samp(x, popmean=100)
stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)   # Welch
stats.ttest_rel(before, after)           # paired
stats.f_oneway(a, b, c, d)               # ANOVA
stats.ansari(a, b)                       # spread
stats.mannwhitneyu(a, b)                 # non-parametric
stats.chi2_contingency(table)            # independence
stats.shapiro(x)                         # normality

res = stats.ttest_1samp(x, 100)
res.statistic, res.pvalue, res.confidence_interval(0.95)

    SciPy defaults ttest_ind to equal_var=True, the less safe choice. R defaults the same function to Welch. Moving code between them silently changes the p-value.

    Report the confidence interval, not only the p-value. The p-value says whether the effect is detectable at this sample size; the interval says whether it is big enough to act on.

    What a p-value is not

    • Not the probability the null hypothesis is true.
    • Not the probability the result happened by chance.
    • Not a measure of effect size — a trivial difference is significant at a large enough n.
    • Not a licence to say "no effect" when it is large. That is "could not detect one".

    p = 0.03 means: if the null were true, data this extreme or more would occur 3% of the time. Everything else people say about p-values is a misreading of that sentence.

    0x0A

    Regression

    In plain terms

    Regression fits a line through your data so you can say how much one thing moves when another moves, and how sure you are of that figure. It is the most useful technique on the syllabus and the one consulting work actually runs on.

    DOM207 module 10, and the technique that earns its keep most often in consulting. statsmodels rather than scikit-learn, because inference needs standard errors and scikit-learn does not report them.

    OLS with a formula

    import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

fit = smf.ols("revenue ~ spend + heads + C(region)",
              data=df).fit()
print(fit.summary())

fit.params; fit.bse; fit.pvalues
fit.conf_int()
fit.rsquared; fit.rsquared_adj
fit.fittedvalues; fit.resid
fit.predict(new_df)

# interaction, and a transformed term
smf.ols("y ~ x * z + np.log(w)", data=df).fit()

    C(region) marks a variable as categorical and builds the dummies with one level held out as reference. x * z expands to x + z + x:z.

    Report adjusted R² alongside R². Plain R² can only rise when a predictor is added — even a column of noise — so it always prefers the bigger model.

    Diagnostics

    ax.scatter(fit.fittedvalues, fit.resid)   # funnel = hetero
sm.qqplot(fit.resid, line="s")            # normality

from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import (
    variance_inflation_factor as vif)
vif(X.values, i)                          # >5 is a warning

from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import het_breuschpagan
het_breuschpagan(fit.resid, fit.model.exog)

robust = fit.get_robustcov_results("HC3")  # the usual fix
fit.get_influence().cooks_distance[0]

    Heteroskedasticity does not bias coefficients — it biases their standard errors, so intervals and p-values are wrong while point estimates are fine. Robust standard errors fix the inference without touching the data.

    Collinearity likewise does not bias coefficients; it inflates their variance, so two collinear predictors each look insignificant while jointly explaining plenty.

    Logistic and other GLMs

    fit = smf.logit("renewed ~ tenure + spend", data=df).fit()
np.exp(fit.params)          # odds ratios
np.exp(fit.conf_int())
fit.prsquared               # McFadden pseudo R2
fit.predict(new_df)         # probabilities

smf.probit("y ~ x", data=df).fit()
smf.poisson("count ~ x", data=df).fit()   # counts
fit.pred_table()            # confusion matrix

    Coefficients are on the log-odds scale; exponentiating gives odds ratios. An odds ratio of 1.06 is a 6% increase in the odds, not in the probability.

    Report a predicted probability for a concrete, named case. "A 24-month customer spending ₹1500 has a 71% chance of renewing" lands where a coefficient table does not.

    The wording that matters

    # wrong
"Spending Rs 1 lakh more CAUSES revenue to rise by 3.2"

# right
"Holding headcount and region fixed, firms spending
 Rs 1 lakh more have on average Rs 3.2 lakh higher
 revenue (95% CI 2.9 to 3.5, n = 150)."

    Observational regression measures association conditional on the variables you included. Causation comes from the design of the study — randomisation, an instrument, a natural experiment — never from the fit.

    "Associated with", "holding fixed", the interval, and the sample size. Four habits that turn a defensible model into a defensible sentence.

    0x0B

    scikit-learn

    In plain terms

    Machine learning, here, means: show the computer many examples where you already know the answer, let it find the pattern, then apply that pattern to new cases. Every tool in this library works the same way — fit to learn, predict to apply.

    DOM207 modules 11 to 13. Every estimator shares one interface — fit, predict, score — so learning one teaches you all of them. The discipline that matters is what you fit on and what you report on.

    The shared interface

    from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=1, stratify=y)

model.fit(Xtr, ytr)
pred = model.predict(Xte)
proba = model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
model.score(Xte, yte)

    Split first, then fit. stratify=y keeps the class balance the same in both halves, which matters whenever the positive class is rare.

    random_state on every split and every model. Without it, two runs of the same script report different accuracies and neither is reproducible.

    Pipelines prevent leakage

    from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# WRONG: scaler sees the test set
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
Xtr, Xte = train_test_split(Xs, ...)

# RIGHT: scaler is fitted inside each fold
pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC())
pipe.fit(Xtr, ytr)

    Fitting a transform on all the data lets test-set statistics influence training. The reported accuracy is then optimistic and will not reproduce on genuinely new data.

    Leakage is the most common cause of a suspiciously good result. If accuracy jumps unexpectedly, look at what was fitted before the split.

    The models on the syllabus

    from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, AgglomerativeClustering
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer

DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3).fit(X, y)
SVC(kernel="rbf", C=1.0, gamma="scale")
KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=1)
PCA().fit(Xs).explained_variance_ratio_
TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english").fit_transform(docs)

    Distance-based methods — SVM with an RBF kernel, k-means, PCA — all require scaled inputs. An unscaled variable with a larger range dominates the distance and the others contribute nothing.

    export_text(tree, feature_names=...) prints the tree as nested rules. That readability is why trees survive in settings where someone must sign off on the logic.

    Metrics, honestly

    from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, precision_score,
    recall_score, f1_score, confusion_matrix,
    classification_report, roc_auc_score,
    mean_squared_error, r2_score)

print(classification_report(yte, pred))
confusion_matrix(yte, pred)      # rows actual

from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5, scoring="f1").mean()

    Accuracy is uninformative under class imbalance: with 9% positives, predicting "no" every time scores 91%. Precision, recall and the confusion matrix are what expose that.

    The 0.5 decision threshold is a choice, not a law. Move it according to the relative cost of a false positive and a false negative — a business question, not a statistical one.

    0x0C

    Gotchas

    In plain terms

    Mistakes that produce no error at all. The program runs, prints a number, and the number is wrong. These are the expensive ones precisely because nothing warns you.

    The mistakes that produce a plausible wrong number rather than an error. These are the expensive ones, because nothing tells you they happened.

    Chained assignment

    # may not do anything at all
df[df.region == "North"]["revenue"] = 0

# correct: one .loc, both axes
df.loc[df.region == "North", "revenue"] = 0

    The chained form selects a subset — potentially a copy — and assigns into that. Under pandas 3's copy-on-write this reliably does nothing to the original, silently.

    One .loc with rows and columns together, always. If you ever see a SettingWithCopyWarning, this is what it is telling you.

    and/or on arrays

    # raises: truth value is ambiguous
df[(df.a > 1) and (df.b < 2)]

# correct, with parentheses
df[(df.a > 1) & (df.b < 2)]
df[~(df.a > 1)]                 # ~ is not

    and and or need a single truth value; an array has many. The element-wise operators are &, | and ~.

    The parentheses are mandatory: & binds tighter than >, so leaving them out compares the wrong things and the error message will not say so.

    Silent alignment

    a = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], index=[0, 1, 2])
b = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=[1, 2, 3])
a + b        # NaN, 12, 23, NaN — aligned by index

# after filtering, indices are no longer 0..n
sub = df[df.x > 5]
sub["new"] = other_series.values   # .values bypasses it

    pandas aligns on the index before every arithmetic operation. Assigning a Series with a different index into a filtered frame produces NaN wherever the labels do not match.

    After a filter, either .reset_index(drop=True) or assign .values. Rows appearing as NaN for no reason is nearly always this.

    Small things that bite

    • df.mean() skips NaN by default; NumPy's mean propagates it. Two functions, two behaviours.
    • np.std() is ddof=0; Series.std() is ddof=1. Same word, different number.
    • sort_values() returns a new frame — assign it or nothing happens.
    • read_csv drops leading zeros from IDs. Pass dtype={"pin": str}.
    • An integer column with any NaN becomes float64. Use Int64 if that matters.
    • Excel dates read as numbers if the column is mixed. Check dtypes immediately.

    After every read, run df.info() and df.isna().sum(). Two lines, and they catch most of this list before it reaches a result.

    ⇆

    The same thing in both languages

    In plain terms

    You already solve every problem in this course twice, once in each language. This is the lookup version of that: when you know the line in one and need it in the other, it is here rather than three sets back.

    Twenty-eight operations, each written both ways. Every fragment here is executed by build/verify_ds.py — preamble plus all twenty-eight in one script per language — so a row that stopped working fails the build rather than sitting here being wrong.

    TaskPythonR
    Read a CSV
    df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
    df <- read.csv("data.csv")
    First few rows
    df.head()
    head(df)
    Types and structure

    The first thing to run after any import, in both languages.

    df.info()
    str(df)
    Rows and columns
    df.shape
    dim(df)
    Column names
    df.columns.tolist()
    names(df)
    Pick columns
    df[["group", "score"]]
    df[, c("group", "score")]      # base
select(df, group, score)       # dplyr
    Pick rows
    df[df.score > 60]
    df[df$score > 60, ]            # base
filter(df, score > 60)         # dplyr
    Add a column
    df["z"] = df.score * 2
    df$z <- df$score * 2           # base
mutate(df, z = score * 2)      # dplyr
    Sort
    df.sort_values("score", ascending=False)
    df[order(-df$score), ]         # base
arrange(df, desc(score))       # dplyr
    Group and aggregate
    df.groupby("group")["score"].mean()
    tapply(df$score, df$group, mean)   # base
df |> group_by(group) |> summarise(m = mean(score))
    Count categories
    df.group.value_counts()
    table(df$group)
    Count missing per column
    df.isna().sum()
    colSums(is.na(df))
    Drop rows with missing
    df.dropna()
    na.omit(df)
    Mean ignoring missing

    The defaults differ. pandas skips NA silently; R returns NA until you ask it not to. Neither is wrong, and neither warns you.

    df.score.mean()                # skipna=True by default
    mean(df$score, na.rm = TRUE)   # NA without this
    Standard deviation

    The single most common cross-language discrepancy in this course. R divides by n−1 always; NumPy divides by n unless told otherwise. pandas already agrees with R.

    df.score.std()                 # ddof=1, agrees with R
np.std(x)                      # ddof=0, does not
    sd(df$score, na.rm = TRUE)     # always n-1
    Join two tables
    df.merge(other, on="id")
    merge(df, other, by = "id")    # base
inner_join(df, other, by = "id")   # dplyr
    Wide to long
    df.melt(id_vars="id", value_vars=["score", "weight"])
    pivot_longer(df, c(score, weight))
    Summary of every column
    df.describe()
    summary(df)
    Correlation of two columns
    df.score.corr(df.weight)
    cor(df$score, df$weight, use = "complete.obs")
    Histogram
    plt.hist(df.score.dropna())
    hist(df$score)
    Scatter plot
    plt.scatter(df.score, df.weight)
    plot(df$score, df$weight)
    Two-group t-test

    R defaults to Welch's test, which does not assume equal variance. SciPy defaults to Student's, which does. Same data, two different p-values, no warning from either.

    a = df[df.group == "A"].score.dropna()
b = df[df.group == "B"].score.dropna()
stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)
    t.test(score ~ group, data = df)
    Chi-square on a table
    stats.chi2_contingency(pd.crosstab(df.group, other.region))
    chisq.test(table(df$group, other$region))
    Linear regression
    m = smf.ols("score ~ weight", data=df).fit()
    m <- lm(score ~ weight, data = df)
    Read the model
    m.summary()
    summary(m)
    Predict on new data
    m.predict(pd.DataFrame({"weight": [70.0]}))
    predict(m, data.frame(weight = 70))
    Fix the random seed

    Do this in every script that samples, splits or simulates. Without it the numbers in your report cannot be reproduced — including by you.

    np.random.seed(42)
    set.seed(42)
    Last element of a vector

    The trap that catches everyone. In R a negative index removes that element; in Python it counts from the end.

    x[-1]      # the last element
    x[-1]      # everything EXCEPT the first
x[length(x)]   # the last element
    ⚖

    Which test do I use

    In plain terms

    A statistical test is a rule for deciding whether a pattern in your sample is strong enough to say something about the world. Which one to use is settled entirely by what kind of data you have and how it was collected — not by which one you happen to remember. Read down the first column until a row describes your situation.

    Keyed on what you have, not on what the test is called — which is the form the question arrives in, and the form the End Sem asks it in.

    What you haveThe testPythonRWhat it assumes
    One numeric sample, compare its mean to a claimed valueOne-sample t-test
    stats.ttest_1samp(x, 100)
    t.test(x, mu = 100)

    Roughly normal, or a sample big enough that it does not matter.

    Two independent groups, numeric outcomeTwo-sample t-test (Welch)
    stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)
    t.test(y ~ g, data = df)

    Independent observations. Welch does not assume equal variance; the R default is Welch and the SciPy default is not.

    Same subjects measured twicePaired t-test
    stats.ttest_rel(before, after)
    t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)

    The pairing is real and the order matches. Using the two-sample test here throws away the pairing and usually hides a real effect.

    Three or more groups, numeric outcomeOne-way ANOVA
    stats.f_oneway(a, b, c)
    summary(aov(y ~ g, data = df))

    Tells you only that some group differs. Which pair differs needs a follow-up test with a correction for multiple comparisons.

    Two categorical variables, is there an associationChi-square test of independence
    stats.chi2_contingency(pd.crosstab(df.a, df.b))
    chisq.test(table(df$a, df$b))

    Expected count of at least 5 in most cells. Below that use Fisher's exact test.

    One categorical variable against expected proportionsChi-square goodness of fit
    stats.chisquare(observed, expected)
    chisq.test(table(df$a), p = c(.5, .3, .2))

    The expected proportions were decided before looking at the data.

    Two numeric variables, how strongly do they move togetherPearson correlation
    stats.pearsonr(x, y)
    cor.test(x, y)

    A straight-line relationship. A perfect U-shape scores near zero, so plot it before you trust the number.

    Same, but the relationship is not a straight lineSpearman rank correlation
    stats.spearmanr(x, y)
    cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman")

    Only that the relationship is consistently increasing or decreasing.

    Two independent groups, clearly not normal or badly skewedMann-Whitney U (Wilcoxon rank-sum)
    stats.mannwhitneyu(a, b)
    wilcox.test(y ~ g, data = df)

    Compares distributions rather than means. Use when the sample is small and visibly skewed, not as a reflex.

    Paired measurements, not normalWilcoxon signed-rank
    stats.wilcoxon(before, after)
    wilcox.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)

    Same pairing requirement as the paired t-test.

    Is this variable normal enoughShapiro-Wilk
    stats.shapiro(x)
    shapiro.test(x)

    On a big sample it rejects normality for deviations too small to matter. A Q-Q plot answers the question better than the p-value does.

    Do two groups have equal varianceF-test / Levene
    stats.levene(a, b)
    var.test(a, b)

    Mostly unnecessary now: use Welch's t-test and the question does not arise.

    Predict a number from one or more columnsLinear regression
    smf.ols("y ~ x1 + x2", data=df).fit()
    lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = df)

    Residuals roughly normal with constant spread, and observations independent. Check the residual plots, not just R².

    Predict a yes/no from one or more columnsLogistic regression
    smf.logit("y ~ x", data=df).fit()
    glm(y ~ x, data = df, family = "binomial")

    The coefficients are log-odds. Exponentiate them before putting them in a sentence.

    Every row assumes the observations are independent, and every test on this page tells you whether an effect is detectable, never whether it is large. Report the effect size and the interval beside the p-value or the sentence is not finished.

    ⚠

    Reading an error message

    In plain terms

    An error message names the rule you broke, not the thing you meant, which is why it reads badly at first. Two habits fix most of it: read the last line of a Python traceback first, because that is the actual error and the lines above are only the route to it — and treat anything that produced no message with more suspicion than anything that crashed.

    Left column is the message as it appears. Every one was produced by running the broken snippet it describes on Python 3.13 with pandas 3.0.5 on this machine — build/verify_errors.py re-runs all ten and fails if the text stops matching.

    The messageWhat it means
     
    ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sklearn'

    The library is not installed, or it is installed somewhere this interpreter is not looking.

    Check which Python is running: import sys; print(sys.executable). Installing into the system Python and running the venv's — or the reverse — is the usual cause, and the message is identical either way.

    NameError: name 'totl' is not defined

    A typo, or a variable used before the line that creates it ran.

    In a notebook this often means the defining cell was never run, or was run and then edited. Restart and Run All settles it.

    TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

    You used + between text and a number.

    Use an f-string: f"n={n}". Python will not guess which one you meant to convert, which is deliberate.

    KeyError: 'revenu'

    A column name that does not exist — a typo, a trailing space in the CSV header, or a different case.

    df.columns.tolist() settles it in one line. Whitespace in headers is invisible and extremely common: df.columns = df.columns.str.strip().

    AttributeError: 'DataFrame' object has no attribute 'colums'.
  Did you mean: 'columns'?

    A misspelled method or attribute.

    Python 3.12+ suggests the nearest name, and the suggestion is nearly always right. Read the whole line before searching for anything.

    IndentationError: expected an indented block after function definition on line 1

    Python uses indentation instead of braces, and the body of a def, if or for must be indented.

    Indent the body by four spaces. Mixing tabs and spaces produces the same error from a block that looks correctly indented on screen.

    ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (3,) (2,)

    Two arrays of different lengths in one operation.

    The two shapes in the message are the whole diagnosis. Note that R would recycle here and return an answer — NumPy refusing is the safer behaviour, and the difference bites when you port code between the two.

    ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'x'

    Converting a column to a number when at least one value is not one.

    pd.to_numeric(col, errors="coerce") turns the offending values into NaN instead of raising — but decide what those rows mean before you do that, because it converts a loud failure into a quiet one.

    KeyError: 'id'

    A merge on a column one of the two frames does not have.

    Use left_on and right_on when the key is spelled differently on each side. The message names the column but not which frame is missing it — check both.

    (no message, and no change)

    Assigning into a filtered slice: sub = df[df.a > 1] then sub["b"] = 0. The original df is untouched.

    On pandas 3.0.5, checked here, copy-on-write is on and this raises nothing at all — older tutorials describing a SettingWithCopyWarning are describing pandas 1. Use df.loc[df.a > 1, "b"] = 0 when you mean to change the original.

    The rows marked silent are the expensive ones. A crash costs you an afternoon; a wrong number that never announced itself goes into the report.

    §

    Glossary

    Fourteen of these are statistics vocabulary and are identical in the other file — DOM207 examines the same concepts in both languages, so defining them twice would be two places to drift apart. The first use of each term in this file links here.

    array

    NumPy's container: many values of one type, held together and operated on as a unit.

    x * 2 doubles every element without a loop. Every other library in the stack takes and returns these.

    AUC

    The area under the ROC curve — a single number summarising how well a classifier separates the two classes.

    0.5 is a coin flip and 1.0 is perfect. It is readable even when the classes are very unbalanced, which plain accuracy is not.

    broadcast

    NumPy stretching a smaller array across a larger one so shapes that are not identical can still be combined.

    It is what lets you subtract one row of means from a whole table. It also silently combines two arrays you did not mean to combine, so check shapes when a result looks odd.

    confidence interval

    A range that would contain the true value in a stated percentage of repeated samples — conventionally 95%.

    It is a statement about the procedure, not about this one interval. Report it alongside every estimate: a coefficient with no interval hides how little you know.

    confusion matrix

    The table of predicted class against actual class.

    Every classification metric is computed from these four counts. Read it before accepting an accuracy figure — 95% accuracy on data that is 95% one class is a model that learned to say one word.

    corpus

    The whole collection of documents you are analysing.

    Text methods count words across the corpus, so what you include in it decides what counts as a common word.

    correlation

    A number from −1 to 1 measuring how tightly two variables move together.

    It says nothing about cause, and it only sees straight-line relationships — a perfect U-shape has a correlation near zero.

    cross-validation

    Splitting the data into parts, training on all but one and testing on the one held out, then rotating which part is held out.

    It gives an honest accuracy estimate without needing a second dataset, and it is what separates a model that learned the pattern from one that memorised the rows.

    DataFrame

    pandas' table: rows, and columns that have names and types.

    It is the object nearly all of this course happens inside. A single column pulled out of one is a Series.

    ddof

    Delta degrees of freedom — the amount subtracted from the sample size in the denominator of a variance calculation.

    The whole reason R and NumPy disagree by default. R's sd() always uses n−1; NumPy's std() uses n unless you pass ddof=1.

    degrees of freedom

    The number of values in a calculation that are actually free to vary.

    Once you have used the data to estimate the mean, one value is determined by the rest — which is why the sample variance divides by n−1 rather than n.

    dendrogram

    The tree diagram produced by hierarchical clustering.

    Where you cut it decides how many clusters you get, and that cut is your judgement call, not the algorithm's.

    dtype

    The type of the values in a NumPy array or a pandas column.

    A column of numbers that arrived with one stray comma becomes dtype object, and then .mean() either fails or silently does something else.

    hyperparameter

    A setting you choose before fitting — the number of clusters, the depth of a tree — as opposed to something the model learns.

    Tuning these on your test data quietly turns the test set into training data, and the accuracy you report stops being honest.

    hypothesis test

    A procedure that asks how surprising your data would be if a stated “nothing happening” assumption were true.

    The assumption is chosen before you look. Choosing it afterwards to fit what you found is the most common way a statistics answer loses marks.

    imputation

    Filling a missing value with an estimate rather than dropping the row.

    It keeps sample size but invents data. Whatever you choose — mean, median, a model — goes in the report with its reason, because it moves every number after it.

    index

    The row labels of a pandas DataFrame or Series.

    pandas aligns on it automatically during arithmetic, which is a feature until two objects have different indexes and you get NaN in every row.

    library

    A collection of code somebody else wrote that you bring in with import.

    pandas, NumPy and scikit-learn are libraries. They are not part of Python and have to be installed first.

    NaN

    Not a Number — the marker pandas and NumPy use for a missing value.

    It is contagious: almost any arithmetic touching it produces NaN, and NaN == NaN is False, so you test with .isna() and never with ==.

    null hypothesis

    The specific “no effect” claim a test is set up to try to reject.

    Failing to reject it is not evidence that it is true — it can equally mean your sample was too small to detect a real effect.

    one-hot

    Turning one categorical column into several 0/1 columns, one per category.

    Models take numbers, and encoding categories as 1, 2, 3 would claim that category 3 is three times category 1.

    outlier

    A value far enough from the rest to be worth treating separately.

    It might be a data-entry error or the most interesting row you have. Deleting it without saying so is the difference between cleaning and fabrication.

    overfitting

    A model that has learned the noise in your particular sample rather than the pattern.

    It scores brilliantly on the data it was fitted to and badly on anything new, which is precisely why accuracy is only meaningful on data the model has never seen.

    p-value

    The probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true.

    It is not the probability the hypothesis is true, and it says nothing about how large the effect is. A tiny p-value on a trivial difference is what a big sample does.

    REPL

    Read-Eval-Print Loop — the interactive prompt where you type one line and see its result immediately.

    Good for checking what something does, bad as a place to keep an analysis: nothing in it is reproducible.

    residual

    The gap between what your model predicted and what actually happened, for one row.

    Nearly every check on a regression is a check on the residuals — if there is still a pattern in them, the model has missed something.

    ROC

    A curve tracing the trade-off between catching true positives and raising false alarms as you move the decision threshold.

    It shows that a classifier is not one thing — it is a dial, and where you set the dial is a decision about which mistake costs more.

    scree

    The plot of how much variance each principal component explains, in order.

    You keep components up to the point the plot flattens out. That elbow is a judgement, and the plot exists so the reader can check yours.

    silhouette

    A score from −1 to 1 for how well each point fits its assigned cluster compared with the nearest other cluster.

    Clustering always returns clusters, however meaningless. This is one of the few ways to argue the ones you found are real.

    stop word

    A very common word — “the”, “and”, “of” — removed before text analysis.

    Removing them stops the results being dominated by words present in every document. Which words count as stop words is a choice that belongs in the writeup.

    stratified

    Splitting data so each part keeps the same class proportions as the whole.

    Without it, a random split of rare-event data can put almost none of the rare class in the training set.

    TF-IDF

    A weighting that raises words frequent in one document and lowers words frequent across all of them.

    It is what stops “the” being the most important word in every document you own.

    traceback

    The report Python prints when something goes wrong, listing the chain of calls that reached the error.

    Read it from the bottom: the last line names what went wrong, and the lines above are the route that got there.

    vectorised

    An operation applied to a whole array or column at once rather than through a loop.

    It is both faster and shorter, and in this course a written loop over a DataFrame is usually a sign the vectorised form was not found yet.

    virtual environment

    A project-local folder holding that project's own copies of its libraries.

    It is why installing something for this course cannot break a different project, and why requirements.txt makes your analysis reproducible elsewhere.

    Welch

    A version of the two-sample t-test that does not assume the two groups have equal variance.

    R's t.test() uses it by default; SciPy's ttest_ind does not unless you pass equal_var=False. Same data, two different answers, and no warning from either.

    How to run them

# in the project venv
./.venv/bin/python problem.py

    Every solution here was executed against the versions listed above before shipping — 39 of 39 in each language. Each is standalone: seeded random data, no external file, no manual step.

    Write something wrong before opening the hint. A solution read before the attempt teaches almost nothing, and the End Sem is closed-book.

    The closed-book layer

    Some sets end in recall questions, collapsed by default. They exist because of how DOM207 is actually graded:

    • Quizzes, 20% — surprise, concept-clearing.
